facts.statement: The holotype of Plotopterum was discovered in 1961 in the San Joaquin Valley of California by Dick Bishop and Ed Mitchell.
facts.quote: The future holotype of Plotopterum was discovered in 1961 in the Pyramid Hill Sand member of the Jewett Sand Formation, in the San Joaquin Valley of California, by Dick Bishop and Ed Mitchell.

facts.statement: In 1985, Hasegawa and Storrs L. Olson redescribed Japanese fossil remains as belonging to the genus Plotopterum.
facts.quote: In 1985, Hasegawa himself, with Storrs L. Olson, redescribed the Japanese remains as belonging to the genus Plotopterum, as Plotopterum sp.

facts.statement: Plotopterum is an extinct genus of flightless seabirds from the North Pacific.
facts.quote: Plotopterum is an extinct genus of flightless seabird of the family Plotopteridae, native to the North Pacific during the Late Oligocene and the Early Miocene.

facts.statement: The only described species of Plotopterum is Plotopterum joaquinensis.
facts.quote: The only described species is Plotopterum joaquinensis.

facts.statement: The genus name Plotopterum combines a prefix meaning 'swimming' with a suffix meaning 'wing'.
facts.quote: The genus name, Plotopterum, is formed from the prefix Plot-, meaning "swimming", and the suffix "-pterum", meaning wing.

facts.statement: The holotype of Plotopterum was roughly the size of a Brandt's cormorant but narrower and more rounded.
facts.quote: The holotype associated with Plotopterum, the humeral end of a left coracoid, was roughly the size of those of the extant Brandt's cormorant, but narrower and more rounded.

facts.statement: The swollen shape of the triosseal area in Plotopterum strengthened the wing for swimming.
facts.quote: The shape of the triosseal area, swollen in its lower portion and narrowed anteroposteriorly, was presumably occupied by the pectoral tendon, and strengthened the wing when the animal was swimming.

facts.statement: Unlike the flightless cormorant, the wings of Plotopterum were heavily specialized for swimming rather than reduced.
facts.quote: Contrary to its distant relative, the flightless cormorant, the wings of Plotopterum were not reduced by the lack of use, but were heavily specialized in swimming

facts.statement: An individual attributed to Plotopterum was approximately the size of a great cormorant.
facts.quote: The almost complete femur tentatively attributed to the genus in 1985, MFM 1800, shared similarities with Anhingidae, and the individual it belonged to was probably smaller than those of its Oligocene relatives, approximately the size of a great cormorant.

facts.statement: Plotopterum lived in the North Pacific during the Late Oligocene and Early Miocene.
facts.quote: Plotopterum is an extinct genus of flightless seabird of the family Plotopteridae, native to the North Pacific during the Late Oligocene and the Early Miocene.

facts.statement: Plotopterum lived between 23.04 and 15.98 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aquitanian to Burdigalian (23.04 to 15.98 million years ago)

facts.statement: Plotopterum was likely limited to coastal waters.
facts.quote: Plotopterum and its close relative Stemec are found in coastal deposits, and were possibly limited to coastal waters

facts.statement: It is suggested that the diversification of marine mammals may have contributed to the extinction of plotopterids.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that the diversification of marine mammals occurring in the Pacific Ocean during the Late Paleogene and the Early Neogene may have concurrenced the plotopterids, and participated in their extinction.

facts.statement: Plotopterum belongs to the family Plotopteridae.
The flightlessness of Plotopterum is inferred rather than confirmed due to a lack of well-preserved remains.
facts.quote: flightlessness can only be inferred due to the lack of well-preserved remains.

facts.statement: It is suggested that the isolation of Plotopterum in Miocene California and Japan allowed it to retain primitive traits.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that the isolation of the ghost lineage limited to the Miocene of California and Japan to which belong Plotopterum, sister taxon to all other plotopterids from the Oligocene of the Pacific Northwest and Japan, may have permitted the preservation of basal traits.
